newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand debt sells at close after RBNZ speech.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand debt sells at close after RBNZ speech.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.35 PCT (PREV 9.45) US 30-YR 6.51 (PREV 6.49)
* NZ debt sells off after slow open
* RBNZ easing still on cards after Brash speech
New Zealand debt markets sold off around nine points across the curve at Monday's close, after a slow start to the session.
Dealers said the currency had suffered after Reserve Bank governor Don Brash called for fiscal restraint to curtail the Kiwi dollar in the aftermath of October's inconclusive general election.

Brash said the continued rapid rise of the kiwi would weaken export growth, and a direct way of reducing the risk inherent in the current situation would be to ensure further fiscal stimulus was not added in the process of forming a political coalition.

The currency ended at US$0.7081/88, down from its 0.7101/08 open. Meanwhile, 90-day bank bill rates climbed nine basis points to 9.17 percent and their futures counterparts fell 15 to 91.24. Three and 10-year bonds were both nine points weaker.
"I guess it's given bonds a bit of a confidence knock," one bond dealer said, adding that the immediate risk was that offshore investors might pull some of their "hot money" out of New Zealand.
Brash said it seemed to have become popular wisdom that investing in NZ dollar assets was a "virtually riskless exercise", and a more realistic understanding of the situation was needed.

"My reading of it is he's saying to offshore investors watch out, you're not necessarily on a sure bet here. It's probably a 'don't be greedy' message, I guess, at the end of the day," the dealer said.
"But I don't think this really changes anything -- there is certainly still room there for easings to come through, and the market should be heartened by that."
A money market dealer agreed.

"If anything he (Brash) is still signalling we're going to have potentially an easing in the interest rate side to alleviate some of these currency pressures. I still think he's hinting along those lines," he said.

The bond dealer said if flows from eurokiwi issues and offshore investors continued coming on shore, the RBNZ may make another statement similar to October 24's, when it said it might have to accept a higher Kiwi and lower rates than were ideal.

"So there's still the chance of another flying of the white flag. We've still got a very real chance of that sort of situation if offshore investors say well, you may want this but the reality is we still like the yields you're offering over there," he said. ---------------------------(SPREADS)----------------------------
